The Toothed flounder, Cyclopsetta querna, is a flatfish species inhabiting the eastern Pacific coastal waters from the Gulf of California to Peru. Field surveys have documented substantial sexual size dimorphism, with females attaining a greater ultimate body length than males. The maximum recorded total length for adult females reaches 43.2 centimeters [Li = 43.2 centimeters], whereas males achieve a smaller asymptotic size of 39 centimeters [Li = 39 centimeters]. This disparity in ultimate length likely arises from differential energetic investment in gamete production, with females directing more resources toward somatic growth to accommodate larger ovarian mass. The length at which the onset of puberty occurs, as indicated by the initiation of gonadal maturation, has been estimated at 21 centimeters [Lp = 21 centimeters] total length, a threshold that marks the transition from the juvenile phase to a reproductively capable state. Individuals below this size are typically immature and allocate little energy toward gametogenesis, focusing instead on somatic development in the productive benthic habitats they occupy after settlement.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], the embryonic development of Cyclopsetta querna proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, is entirely lecithotrophic and relies on endogenous yolk reserves for its initial nutritional requirements. The wet weight at birth for these freshly hatched individuals is extraordinarily low, measured at 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams], a mass that reflects the small diameter of the pelagic egg from which they emerge. This minuscule initial size places the larvae among the most diminutive of the Paralichthyidae, demanding exceptionally high feeding success during the exotrophic transition once the yolk sac is fully absorbed. The timing of this critical hatching event is highly sensitive to thermal conditions, and the relatively warm incubation temperature of 26.8 °C accelerates developmental rates compared to cooler regimes typical of more northern flatfish species.

As the larvae progress through the pelagic larval phase and undergo the dramatic morphological transformation of metamorphosis, they eventually settle to the benthos as juveniles and begin the slow trajectory toward their ultimate adult dimensions. Based on length-weight relationships derived for the species, the wet weight corresponding to the onset of puberty is approximately 115 grams [Wwp = approximately 115 grams], a value that integrates the length at first maturity with the allometry of body mass. This mass represents a substantial increase from the newborn condition, illustrating the rapid growth achieved during the early juvenile period. For adults that have completed somatic growth, the ultimate wet weight for females, derived from the asymptotic length of 43.2 centimeters, is approximately 1000 grams [Wwi = approximately 1000 grams]. This maximum body weight places Cyclopsetta querna among the medium-sized members of its genus, and maintaining such a mass requires efficient foraging on the crustacean and small fish prey that dominate its diet.

The reproductive output of the Toothed flounder has been characterized from field collections of gravid females, yielding estimates of the maximum fecundity. At the thermal conditions of the wild populations, which average 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], females produce a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year], releasing an estimated 210000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 210000 eggs per spawning event] during the peak of the spawning season. This annual fecundity places this species among the more productive tropical flatfishes, compensating for the high mortality experienced by the tiny, planktonic eggs and yolk-sac larvae. The trade-off between investment in individual egg size and total fecundity is evident, as the egg diameter of about 1 millimeter yields the very low wet weight at birth.

The natural lifespan of Cyclopsetta querna has been estimated from otolith-based age readings and mark-recapture studies in the Gulf of California. The maximum recorded longevity for the species is 7 years [am = 7 years] when reared under the ambient thermal conditions of its native habitat, where water temperatures average approximately 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C]. This lifespan is relatively moderate compared to many deeper-water pleuronectiforms, which can exceed 20 years, but it is typical for a warm-water flatfish with a fast growth rate and early onset of reproduction. Senescence likely sets in after the fifth year, as reproductive output shows a decline in older individuals, though the precise age-related changes in physiology remain poorly documented. The combination of early maturity at 21 centimeters and a moderate maximum age allows the species to maintain stable populations despite the high natural mortality rates experienced during the fragile larval and early juvenile phases.
